prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Shell plc" (ticker SHEL), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "SHEL", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Shell plc
markets: Liquefied natural gas (LNG) production and trading
Power, low-carbon fuels and carbon capture

mission.statement: Our purpose is to power progress together by working with each other, our customers and our partners to provide the energy products people need to power their lives and businesses.
mission.source: Shell plc Annual Report and Accounts 2025
mission.plain: Shell wants to work with others to supply the energy people and businesses need every day.

about.plain: Shell pumps oil and natural gas out of the ground and from under the sea. It cools gas into a liquid so it can be shipped across oceans, and it is the world's biggest seller of this liquid gas. It turns oil into petrol, diesel, jet fuel, motor oil and chemicals, and sells fuel at Shell petrol stations around the world. It also buys and sells energy as a huge trader.
about.customers: Drivers, airlines, shipping companies, power plants, factories and whole countries that need fuel and gas.
about.everyday: The yellow-and-red Shell petrol stations and Pennzoil and Shell Helix motor oils are familiar to drivers in many countries.

money.plain: fuel, motor oil and shop sales at Shell stations
making and trading fuels and chemicals
gas cooled to a liquid and shipped worldwide
crude oil and gas from Brazil, the Gulf of Mexico, Nigeria and the North Sea

money.part: Canadian Montney gas and liquids (ARC Resources)
money.plain: gas and liquids from western Canada, bought in September 2026
storing CO2 underground and making cleaner fuels

result.summary: Shell sells commodities at market prices, so it has little pricing power; its edge is scale and position, above all the world's largest LNG portfolio and trading business, which lets it profit from moving gas between regions. Its retail brand is the most valuable in the oil and gas sector, and its deepwater know-how in Brazil and the Gulf of Mexico is hard to copy. The result is a narrow but real moat in a cyclical industry, now refocused under CEO Wael Sawan on LNG and oil rather than renewables.

pricingPower.evidence: Revenue tracks oil and gas prices Shell does not set: it went from $180,543M in 2020 to $381,314M in 2022, fell to $266,886M in 2025, then hit $94,664M in Q2 2026 alone when Middle East disruption sent prices up; its premium V-Power fuels and Helix lubricants are the only products that carry a price premium.

moats.evidence: Brand Finance ranked Shell the world's most valuable oil and gas brand for the eleventh year running in 2025 ($45.4 billion, brand strength 87.5/100), helping its stations, V-Power fuel and lubricants earn a modest premium.
Drivers and most industrial buyers switch fuel suppliers freely; only long-term LNG supply contracts and fleet fuel-card deals tie customers in for years.

Its global LNG portfolio gains some flexibility as it adds supply sources and buyers (it replaced lost Qatari volumes in 2026 with Nigeria, Trinidad, LNG Canada and third-party cargoes), but this is a scale benefit more than a true network effect.

It is the largest LNG portfolio player, produced 2,800 thousand boe/d in 2025 and is targeting $5-7 billion of structural cost cuts, which gives it buying, shipping and trading scale few rivals match.
LNG plants such as LNG Canada (full capacity in 2026) and deepwater hubs cost tens of billions of dollars and take years to build, limiting how many competitors can enter each project.
Shell competes with the same integrated model as ExxonMobil, Chevron, TotalEnergies and BP, and has retreated from its earlier renewables push.
Decades of deepwater execution in Brazil and the Gulf of Mexico, gas-to-liquids technology at Pearl GTL in Qatar and an integrated trading operation linked to its refineries are hard to replicate.
Long-life stakes in Qatar LNG, Brazil's pre-salt fields, LNG Canada and, since September 2026, ARC Resources' Montney acreage are scarce assets, though partners and host governments share them.

customers.evidence: Shell has the strongest brand in the sector and loyalty programmes such as Shell Go+, but most of its fuel, gas and chemicals are bought on price under commodity contracts, and it closed or sold about 800 weaker retail sites in 2025.

talent.evidence: With about 85,000 employees it still attracts strong engineers, traders and geoscientists, but repeated job cuts under the cost programme and the industry's falling appeal to young graduates weigh on its employer standing.

product.evidence: Shell V-Power fuels and Helix/Pennzoil lubricants are well regarded and its LNG trading is seen as best in class, but crude oil, gas and most refined products are interchangeable commodities.

competitors.name: Exxon Mobil (ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation)
competitors.note: Largest Western integrated major; competes in upstream, LNG, refining, chemicals and lubricants (Mobil 1).

competitors.name: TotalEnergies SE
competitors.note: European integrated major and Shell's closest rival in LNG portfolio trading, fuel retail and power.

competitors.name: BP p.l.c.
competitors.note: UK integrated major competing in upstream, refining, fuel retail, trading and LNG.

competitors.name: Chevron Corporation
competitors.note: US integrated major competing in deepwater, Australian LNG, refining and fuel retail.

competitors.name: QatarEnergy
competitors.note: State-owned largest LNG exporter and Shell's partner in Qatar; competes for LNG buyers worldwide.

competitors.name: Saudi Arabian Oil Company (Saudi Aramco)
competitors.note: World's largest oil producer, expanding in gas, refining, chemicals and lubricants (Valvoline).

competitors.name: Equinor ASA
competitors.note: Competes in North Sea production, European gas supply and Brazilian offshore.

competitors.name: Petróleo Brasileiro S.A. (Petrobras)
competitors.note: Shell's operator-partner in Brazil's pre-salt fields and a rival for deepwater acreage.

competitors.name: Cheniere Energy, Inc.
competitors.note: Largest US LNG exporter competing for long-term LNG supply contracts.

competitors.name: Woodside Energy Group Ltd
competitors.note: Australian LNG producer competing for Asian LNG buyers.

competitors.name: Eni S.p.A.
competitors.note: Italian integrated company competing in African gas, LNG and European fuels.

competitors.name: Vitol Group
competitors.note: World's largest independent energy trader, competing with Shell's oil, gas and LNG trading arm.

competitors.name: Trafigura Group
competitors.note: Independent commodity trader competing in oil and LNG trading.

competitors.name: PetroChina Company Limited
competitors.note: Chinese state-controlled oil and gas giant and major LNG buyer and trader.

competitors.name: Couche-Tard (Alimentation Couche-Tard Inc.)
competitors.note: Circle K owner competing with Shell's fuel and convenience retail network.

threats: Oil and gas price swings: 2026 profits were lifted by the Middle East supply shock, which could reverse as volatility eases.
Damage and shipping disruption around the Strait of Hormuz cut Shell's Qatar LNG and Pearl GTL volumes in 2026; one Pearl train may not return until Q1 2027.
A wave of new LNG supply (about 180 million tonnes expected by 2030) could squeeze LNG prices and trading margins.
Long-term decline in oil demand from electric vehicles and climate policy, plus litigation and campaigner pressure over emissions.
Integration risk and higher share count from the $13.9 billion ARC Resources acquisition, and execution on LNG Canada Phase 2.
Weak European refining and chemicals margins and windfall taxes in the UK and EU.

ceo.name: Wael Sawan
ceo.background: Chemical engineer (McGill MEng) with a Harvard MBA; joined Shell in 1997 and ran Qatar Shell and the Integrated Gas and Renewables division

c1.evidence: Shell leads LNG, a growing market, but its overall industry of oil, gas and fuels is mature rather than emerging, and its revenue fell from $381,314M in 2022 to $266,886M in 2025.

c2.evidence: Customers choose Shell mainly for location, reliability and supply security (its LNG portfolio kept cargoes flowing when Qatar went offline in 2026), an advantage of scale that is durable but not unique among majors.

c3.evidence: The Shell pecten is recognised worldwide and Brand Finance rates it the most valuable oil and gas brand, but it is not the clear default choice the way Google is, and few people actively recommend an oil company.

c4.evidence: Its purpose to "power progress together" is broad, and under Wael Sawan the company has openly prioritised returns and buybacks over its earlier energy-transition ambitions, selling its European onshore renewables to TotalEnergies in 2026.

c6.evidence: “oil giant, petrol stations, polluter, profitable” – people know and trust the brand at the pump, but public opinion of Shell as a company is mixed to negative because of climate and environmental controversies such as the Niger Delta.

c7.evidence: Global energy demand is huge and LNG demand is expected to grow about 65% by 2050 per Shell's outlook, but oil, its other core market, faces long-term decline rather than a secular boom.

c8.evidence: Shell can expand in LNG (LNG Canada Phase 2, ARC's Montney gas) and in trading and power, but it has stepped back from large new low-carbon markets such as renewables and hydrogen.

m1.evidence: Wael Sawan has a clear, pragmatic view that LNG and oil will be needed for decades and has refocused Shell on them, but this is a disciplined strategy rather than a bold vision of the future.

m2.evidence: Sawan is a 29-year Shell career executive, not a founder, and his focus on quarterly buybacks and closing the valuation gap with US peers reflects shareholder priorities more than founder-style building.

m4.evidence: He has emphasised performance and simplicity, cutting jobs and costs (targeting $5-7 billion of structural savings), which serves shareholders more visibly than employees.

m5.evidence: Sawan's cultural push is about performance, discipline and cost cutting rather than a culture of inventing new products, and Shell has cut low-carbon R&D and new-energy ventures.

m6.evidence: He is a chemical engineer who started as a field engineer in Oman and ran Qatar's LNG and Pearl GTL operations, so he knows the operations well, though as CEO he focuses on portfolio and capital allocation.

m7.evidence: There are no character scandals, but his stewardship is centred on shareholder returns, including scrapping Shell's plan to cut oil output each year, which critics see as putting profit ahead of climate goals.

m7b.evidence: No record was found of Wael Sawan giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Sawan is known as a measured, numbers-focused executive rather than a distinctive public personality.

m9.evidence: Since he took over in January 2023 Shell has met cost targets, kept buybacks of at least $3 billion a quarter, cut net debt to $41,754M by June 2026 and delivered Q2 2026 adjusted earnings of $9,836M with record refinery utilisation.

m10.evidence: Sawan has driven a strict cost programme and job cuts, but Shell is not known for a frugal culture and his 2025 pay rose about 60% to £13.8 million.

c10.evidence: Shell's fuel, gas and lubricants keep cars, planes, homes and factories running for around a billion people a year, but they are commodities others could supply and they add to carbon emissions.

p2.evidence: Building LNG plants such as LNG Canada and deepwater platforms in Brazil takes tens of billions of dollars and rare engineering skill, and reliable energy supply is critical to the world economy.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose from $180,543M in 2020 to $381,314M in 2022, then fell each year to $316,620M in 2023, $284,312M in 2024 and $266,886M in 2025.

f2.evidence: Net margin improved from a loss in 2020 (attributable loss of $21,680M) to 6.7% in 2025, but it peaked in 2022 at about 11% and Shell does not report gross or operating margins.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 Shell had $31,374M of cash against $73,076M of debt including $29,627M of leases, with gearing of 18.7% and equity of $181,781M, which is manageable given $27,495M of first-half operating cash flow but not low.

f4.evidence: Profit rose from a 2020 loss to $17,838M in 2025, but operating cash flow peaked at $68,414M in 2022 and fell to $42,863M in 2025 before rebounding to $27,495M in the first half of 2026.

v1.evidence: Shell fuel is comparable to rivals' and drivers mostly pick a station by price and convenience; only its LNG trading is widely seen as best in class.

v2.evidence: Shell is a well-known employer for engineers and traders, but it does not appear on global best-places-to-work lists such as Fortune's, and it has been cutting jobs under its cost programme.

c5.evidence: Drivers, airlines and countries that rely on its LNG, such as those in Europe and Asia in 2026, would notice a sudden shortage, but other suppliers would gradually fill the gap and the world would gain from lower emissions.
